title: Life Games

source.quote: Jack is playing the game called Kick Me.

setting: A week of catching up with old friends, one at a time, and noticing the same shapes keep showing up.

L1.line: Yeah, I knew she'd bail eventually. They always do.
cues: fourth breakup, same line as the last three
L1.question: Omar grumbles to his drinking buddies about yet another breakup - same story as the last three, same shrug at the end, everyone at the bar nodding along. Is this Kick Me at the first, second, or third degree?

options.feedback: Right. A first-degree game has an outcome the player is willing to share with his social circle - first-degree games make up a large share of time-structuring at bars and parties. Omar is grumbling openly, and the room treats it as completely normal.

Not quite - second-degree outcomes are heavier, ones the player would rather keep private. Omar is telling this story to a room full of friends over drinks, not hiding it from anyone - that openness is what actually marks this as first degree instead.

Not quite - third degree, in Berne's words, ends "in the surgery, the courtroom or the morgue." Nobody here is hurt or in legal trouble, this is much lighter than that - casual and public is the mark of first degree instead.

L1.lesson: Degree isn't about how often you play; it's about how publicly you can survive the outcome. First degree stays shareable at a bar; second degree gets hidden from your social circle; third degree, in Berne's words, "...is one which is played for keeps, and which ends in the surgery, the courtroom, or the morgue."

L2.intro: Same week, three different friends, three different Life Games - and one that needs a whole cast of five to run: the Alcoholic game, which shows up later in the questions below.

beats.line: Of course she left. They always leave eventually. Guess I'm just not relationship material.

options.text: Aw, don't say that, you're great, she didn't deserve you.
options.outcome: Omar perks up for a second, then sighs. "Yeah, well. Story of my life." The same shrug returns within the hour.
options.lesson: Comforting the "I'm not-OK" belief feels supportive and quietly confirms it - he collects the sympathy as more evidence for the same script.

options.text: You keep ending up back here. What do you think you do, before it gets to the leaving part?
options.outcome: Long pause. "I mean... I do pick fights right when things are going well. Huh."
options.lesson: Asking what his own part in the repeat pattern is - without supplying the kick, without rescuing him from the question - is the opening that lets him see the game instead of just re-feeling it.

options.text: Honestly? Maybe you ARE doing something wrong.
options.outcome: Omar's face falls exactly the way it fell with her. "Yeah. Figured you'd say that too." Kick delivered, right on schedule.
options.lesson: This hands him the exact kick his game was built to collect - Persecutor to his Victim, completing the Payoff instead of interrupting it.

beats.line: I knew it. I KNEW he'd do this eventually. I've got three months of texts proving he never cared. We're done.
cues: "I knew it" said with satisfaction, not sadness
pulls out a saved folder of evidence

options.text: Wow, yeah, show me everything, he's the worst.
options.outcome: Leah lights up, scrolling faster. You spend the next hour co-signing the verdict; she looks almost cheerful by the end.
options.lesson: Joining the Persecutor case confirms the collected evidence was worth collecting - it's fun in the room, and it reloads Leah's "I'm OK, you're not-OK" position for the next relationship.

options.text: You've been saving these up for a while, huh.
options.outcome: Leah stops scrolling. "...Yeah. I guess I have." First flicker of noticing the collection itself.
options.lesson: Naming the collecting, not the content, is the Adult cross here - it points at the stamp book instead of grading the evidence inside it.

options.text: Maybe give him a chance to explain before you decide that.
options.outcome: "Don't you dare take his side," Leah snaps, and now you're also on trial.
options.lesson: Technically reasonable, and it answers the wrong question - Leah isn't actually deciding anything; the verdict was reached months ago. This moment is Formula G's Switch, not a search for fresh facts.

beats.line: See, THIS is what happens! Now look what you made me do!
cues: the glass broke because she was mid-yell, waving her arm
blames the kid for her own spilled glass

options.text: He really shouldn't leave his stuff around like that.
options.outcome: Divya nods hard. "Exactly! Thank you!" The kid gets sent to his room; Divya never notices whose hand actually hit the glass.
options.lesson: Validating the blame hands Divya her Payoff cleanly - she gets to be the reasonable Persecutor, with responsibility fully relocated onto the kid.

options.text: Hang on - the glass went over when you were waving your arm, not when he did anything.
options.outcome: Divya opens her mouth to argue, stops. "I... okay, that's fair, that's fair." She actually looks at the glass.
options.lesson: Pointing at the literal mechanics of what happened, flatly, is enough to interrupt See What You Made Me Do - the game depends on nobody checking the physical facts.

options.text: You seem really stressed, let me help clean this up.
options.outcome: You clean the glass. Divya's shoulders relax, already composing the next version of this story for later.
options.lesson: Helpful and kind, and it doesn't touch the blame-shift at all - the mess gets fixed, the belief that it was the kid's fault doesn't.

beats.line: I'll pay you back the second this freelance thing comes through, I swear, you know I'm good for it.
cues: the freelance thing has been "coming through" for two years
introduces himself to new people by joking about how broke he is

options.text: Don't worry about it, seriously, whenever works.
options.outcome: Farid relaxes completely. "You're the only one who gets it." The debt becomes permanent furniture in the friendship.
options.lesson: Lifting the deadline removes the one thing that could ever end the game - Debtor needs an unpaid balance to keep structuring the relationship around.

options.text: I need an actual date, even a bad one, by Friday.
options.outcome: Farid blinks - no joke ready for this one. "Oh. Uh... Friday. Okay. Let me actually check."
options.lesson: A real deadline does what sympathy can't: it forces the balance to become a fact in the room instead of a permanent mood.

options.text: This is getting ridiculous, you need to grow up.
options.outcome: Farid laughs it off - "yeah, yeah, story of my life" - and somehow the joke absorbs the criticism without anything changing.
options.lesson: True, and delivered as judgment rather than a request, it gives him a new self-deprecating bit to perform instead of a deadline to meet.

fields.label: Pick one of the four games above (Kick Me, NIGYSOB, See What You Made Me Do, or Debtor) and write its six advantages: internal psychological, external psychological, internal social, external social, biological, and existential.

Alcoholic is played with five roles, not two: Alcoholic, Persecutor, Rescuer, Patsy, and Connection. In under 40 words, who plays Patsy and Connection in a real drinking circle, and why does the game run longer when both are filled by different people?

echo.setting: A week later. Omar texts about a new breakup, same four months, same shrug in text form.
echo.line: lol of course. you've heard this one before
